Subject-Specific Content & Key ExamplesPlan before draftingpurpose and audiencetext structurekey ideaslanguage and image choicesA clear plan reduces random ideas and supports a complete text.Edit in layersmeaningstructuresentencesspelling and punctuationCheck important content before correcting surface features.Sort and noticeSort planning cards for imaginative, informative and persuasive texts.Guided practiceSort and notice — Sort planning cards for imaginative, informative and persuasive texts.Build or improve — Draft one paragraph, then complete a focused edit for meaning and sentence quality.Explain your choice — Use the words purpose, draft, edit to explain what you changed and why.Three complete original text modelsStory for a classmate — The missing note. Mila carried a note to the school garden. A breeze blew it under a bench. She asked Amir to help, and he found it beside a plant pot. Mila thanked him and put the note safely in her bag.Information for a new classmate — Our model class library.Where books go: Our class library has two shelves. Story books go on the upper shelf. Information books go on the lower shelf.How to return them: Put a book back with its cover facing the front. This helps the next reader see its title.Request to our teacher — A reading box. Please put a reading box beside the mat. We could choose books without crossing the room, and we could return them after quiet reading. A box there would help our class find a book. Could we try it this week?These are invented teaching situations. Notice the story’s linked events, the information headings and the request with a relevant reason. Sort the planning cards below by their purpose, then explain a match.Planning cards to sort and useCard A: Reader: a classmate. Purpose: entertain. Plan: a paper hat blows away; a friend catches it; the owner puts it away safely. Write a linked story with an ending.Card B: Reader: a new classmate. Purpose: inform. Supplied model facts: the art tray is by the window; clean pencils go in the blue pot; used scrap paper goes in the paper box. Group the facts under useful headings.Card C: Reader: the teacher. Purpose: persuade. Request a quiet drawing corner. Give a relevant reason and a polite action to try.Check the planning matchesA is imaginative story writing, B is informative writing and C is persuasive writing. Each requires an actual short written text. For C, accept different relevant reasons rather than one fixed opinion.Sentences and word choicesSimple: The small seed tray was resting on the shelf.Noun group: The small seed tray. The words work together to name and describe a thing. Whole verb group: was resting. Keep both words when identifying what was happening.Compound: The soil was dry, so Mila added water. “The soil was dry” and “Mila added water” can each stand alone; so links the first situation to its result.Contrast: Mila packed seeds and soil. And joins two things here, not two complete messages. A comma is not needed just because and appears.Word bank: seed tray, soil, shelf, basket, garden, paper. Basket, garden and paper each have two syllables in the model’s ordinary pronunciation. Say the word, notice familiar sound–letter patterns and check its conventional spelling.An edit you can explainDraft: “mila took a thing to the garden. She put it it on the shelf”Intended meaning: Mila carries a seed tray. She puts it on the shelf in the garden.Revised: “Mila took a seed tray to the garden. She put it on the shelf.”Replace thing with seed tray so the reader knows the object.Delete the repeated it; keep one it to refer to the seed tray.Add the opening capital and final full stop.Read it back: do the actions stay in a sensible order, and do the words still convey the intended meaning?Create and edit a simple digital textWith an adult, use a familiar drawing or document tool. Create two pages or panels: first Mila carries the seed tray; next she puts it on the shelf. Type a caption for each and draw a matching picture. Use these original starting captions: “Mila carries a seed tray.” and “She puts it on the shelf.”Create the two panels and captions.Check their order. If the shelf panel comes first, move it after the carrying panel.Replace an unclear word, such as thing, with seed tray; delete any repeated word and check capitals and full stops.Read the changed text with the adult. Check each picture matches its caption.Save locally with adult help. Share it only with the agreed familiar reader.A paper drawing-and-caption version practises the same text choices. The digital elaboration requires actually making and revising a digital version; describing a button alone does not demonstrate it.

sections.label: Subject-Specific Content & Key Examples
sections.final_normalized_text: Subject-Specific Content & Key Examples2. Subject-Specific Content & Key ExamplesCheck the main handwriting featurescorrect starting pointconsistent letter sizespaces between wordsletter bodies follow the baseline; some parts reach below itSpeed should increase only while letter formation remains clear.Practise patterns in meaningful wordslower-case familiesupper-case formstwo-syllable wordsshort sentencesBrief focused practice is more useful than long careless copying.Sort and noticeSort letters by similar movement patterns and practise one family.Guided practiceSort and notice — Sort letters by similar movement patterns and practise one family.Build or improve — Copy a short sentence, then circle one strength and one improvement goal.Explain your choice — Use the words legible, formation, spacing to explain what you changed and why.Prepare a real handwriting modelHave suitable paper, a comfortable pencil or agreed adapted writing tool, and a nearby model in the learner’s school-taught unjoined script. An adult writes the target words slowly using that model, showing the actual starting points and movements. The learner watches, then writes beside it without tracing. The typed words here identify the targets only; they do not provide a stroke-order model.Use the preferred writing hand. Adjust paper position and support the paper with the other hand if helpful. Look for comfortable control during writing, following individual school or specialist advice. Do not insist that every learner use one finger arrangement.Complete handwriting targetsCase comparison: Mia and mia. The first can be a person’s name; the second is a case-comparison target. Watch the adult’s local-script capital M and lower-case m.Word targets: Sam; bag; paper; garden. Watch each adult-written model and write it yourself with unjoined letters.Sentence targets: Mia has a blue bag. / Sam has a red mug. / We put a bag here.Copy one short target at a time beside the real model. Check the intended letter order, case, recognisable forms and word spaces. The task supplies the spellings so attention can stay on handwriting.Check relative size and placementAn adult demonstrates a, b, g and B in the learner’s taught style on suitable lines. Compare the short body of a, the tall part of b and the part of g below the baseline. Capital B has a different form from lower-case b. Exact shapes follow the school model.Then the adult writes “a big bag”. The learner copies it. Ask the adult to point to a readable short letter, a tall letter, a part below the baseline and the spaces between the three words. Keep letters within a word together, with clearer word gaps.The baseline is a guide to placement. It does not mean forcing all parts of all letters above it. Use adapted guides if these support comfortable readable writing.Compare actual attempts over timeWrite the adult-modelled sentence “Mia has a blue bag.” Keep the dated sample. Circle one clear word and choose a target, such as the gap after has or the taught movement for b. Practise that feature briefly, then use it in the sentence.In a later short session, repeat under similar conditions with the same useful model and tools. Compare recognisable forms, word gaps, hesitation, comfort and effort. An adult observes actual movement and grasp when these are being discussed. Better ease with readable words is more useful than rushing.Note support and changed conditions. Two attempts made immediately after modelling show current practice; a series of comparable samples helps discuss growth. Stop if there is pain or strain.

sections.label: Learning goals
sections.final_normalized_text: Learning goals1. Outcome Overview & Core ConceptsWords can be analysed as sequences of phonemes. Readers and writers blend sounds, segment words and create new words by deleting or substituting one sound.Big idea: Blend, segment, delete and substitute phonemesLearning routine: Say word → Stretch sounds → Manipulate phoneme → Blend → Check word

Subject-Specific Content & Key ExamplesChange one phonemestopstop → topDeleting /s/ from stop leaves top; the remaining phonemes blend in order.Substitute a soundshipchange /sh/ to /ch/chipcheck meaningSay the new word and confirm that only the intended sound changed.Sort and noticeMove counters for each sound, then remove or replace one counter.Guided practiceSort and notice — Move counters for each sound, then remove or replace one counter.Build or improve — Build word chains by changing one phoneme at a time.Explain your choice — Use the words phoneme, segment, substitute to explain what you changed and why.Complete sound-card routineUse counters or finger taps, not small loose objects with a learner who might put them in their mouth. The adult models fresh: /f/, /r/, the vowel in bed, /sh/. Four phonemes need four counters. The letters sh spell one sound; f and r in the cluster are separate sounds. Show fresh after the spoken model.For a two-syllable model, say cloudy naturally and clap its two syllables. Then segment five phonemes with counters: /k/, /l/, the vowel in cloud, /d/, the final vowel in happy. Do not treat a whole syllable as one phoneme.Adult oral-task card · keep the screen away from the learnerSay each word clearly and give only the spoken instruction. Do not read its answer first. 1. “Say slip without the first /s/.” 2. “Say best without /s/.” 3. “Say tent without the final /t/.” 4. “Say clap. Change the final /p/ to /m/.”Check the oral tasks1. Lip. 2. Bet, keeping final /t/. 3. Ten. 4. Clam. Observe what the learner actually says; reteach only the changed sound if needed. A supplied model counts as support.Build, improve and explain a word chainAdult models the spoken chain slam → slim → swim. First swap the vowel in cat for the vowel in sit. Next swap /l/ for /w/. All other sounds stay in order at each change. After the oral turns, show the print, write each word and reread it. Explain where the phoneme was changed.For a fresh turn, the adult uses a different card from the formative check below with print covered. Reading this displayed chain is useful practice, but does not establish independent oral manipulation.

sections.label: Subject-Specific Content & Key Examples
sections.final_normalized_text: Subject-Specific Content & Key Examples2. Subject-Specific Content & Key ExamplesMap sounds to graphemesrainrainai = the long a soundThe vowel digraph ai represents one vowel phoneme.Notice clusters, silent letters and compoundsfrog: fr clusterknee: silent ksunset: sun + setrobot: two syllablesUse both sound knowledge and known spelling patterns.Sort and noticeSort words by vowel digraph, consonant cluster, silent letter or compound word.Guided practiceSort and notice — Sort words by vowel digraph, consonant cluster, silent letter or compound word.Build or improve — Map phonemes to graphemes in one- and two-syllable words.Explain your choice — Use the words phoneme, grapheme, pattern to explain what you changed and why.Complete reading and sorting cardsRead these cards: green, moon, book, rain, play, beach, bread, night, frog, crisp, knee, thumb, raincoat, sunset, rabbit. Point to the spelling that supports each reading. Sort by vowel pattern, consonant cluster, silent letter or compound. Some words can fit more than one group.Check the sort and explain the overlapsExamples: green has ee; moon and book have oo with different vowel sounds; rain has ai; play has ay; beach and bread have ea with different vowel sounds; night has igh for long i plus final /t/. Frog begins /f/ and /r/; crisp begins /k/ and /r/ and keeps /s/ and /p/ at the end. Knee has silent k; thumb has silent b. Raincoat and sunset are compounds. Rabbit has two syllables but is not built from two complete words.Map, write and rereadModel rain as r | ai | n: three phonemes. Model thumb as th | u | mb: three phonemes in the usual pronunciation, with b not pronounced separately. Model robot by reading its two syllables and joining them. These are sound and spelling models, not three universal rules for every word.Adult dictation card · hide all printed targetsChoose a word whose patterns the learner has been taught. Say “tail” in “The dog wagged its tail”; “bright” in “The lamp is bright”; or “sunhat” in “I packed my sunhat”. The learner says the word, maps its sounds, writes it and reads the spelling back. Say the target word and its sentence aloud. Keep the printed word hidden and do not name its letters or show its spelling until the learner has written it.Check the writingTail uses ai; bright keeps the /b/ and /r/ cluster and igh for long i; sunhat combines sun and hat. Check the actual letters, not only whether the learner can select a printed answer.

Point to the unusual part: ai in said and ie in friend spell the vowel in bed. Come and have show that final e does not always signal a long vowel. Read each whole word and its useful consonant clues.Compare one, once, only and lone with an adult’s spoken model. One and once begin with a /w/ sound despite having no written w; only and lone have the long o vowel. Compare their exact spellings without treating them as a simple rule for adding one suffix to every word.Check the model analysisMap the useful sounds before marking the unexpected part. The same ai spelling can represent different vowels in rain and said; the same short vowel can be written differently in said and friend. Keep the known base friend when writing friendly.Complete related-word and context tasksRead these pairs: jump → jumped; play → played; want → wanted. Read “The wind shook the branch” and “Please wind the toy”, attending to the meaning and all the printed letters.Check the word parts and readingHelpful means giving help; played marks that the playing happened in the past; jumping names the ongoing action in “I am jumping.” The bases help, play and jump remain visible. Painted keeps paint and adds ed, which adds a syllable here. Check exact written forms some and painted; an analogy prompt is support and should be recorded.

They create word families and change meaning, grammar or both.Big idea: Build related words by adding meaningful partsLearning routine: Find base → Add prefix or suffix → Read new word → Explain new meaning

Prefixes: re, un. Suffixes: er, ful, ing, ed, ness, ly, ship. Make conventional words and explain them in a sentence; do not assume every card joins to every base.Meaningful families to read and extendBaseFamily examplesExplain the changehelphelper, helpful, helpingA person, a helpful quality, or an ongoing actionkindunkind, kindnessNot kind; the quality of being kindfriendfriendly, friendshipActing like a friend; a relationship between friendscovercovering, uncoverThe action in “I am covering”; reverse the coveringPosition and meaning both matter when building a family.Sort the affix cards by position: re and un go before a base; these suffix cards go after. Use the actual meaning of each finished word to check your choice.Family boundary checkCompare play, replay, player and day. Compare kind, unkind and nice: nice can have a similar meaning, but does not contain kind.Check and explainA morphemic family needs a shared meaningful base, not just matching sounds or a similar meaning.
